Physiological and psychological responses and cognitive
performance with a window view
KUNIAKI MIHARA(cid:1), TAKAMASA HASAMA and HIROYUKI TAKASUNA
Kajima Corporation, Kajima Technical Research Institute Singapore, Singapore, Singapore
A window view, including nature, decreases stress and improves well-being. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of a
window view on physiological and psychological responses and cognitive performance. Twenty-six participants were exposed to two
viewing conditions (closed blinds and window view) in real and virtual environments. Skin temperature, skin conductance, heart-rate
variability, and electroencephalography were examined. Cognitive tests were conducted for the participants after an environmental
exposure for 5min. During the exposure and tests, participants with a window view recorded higher skin temperature, lower skin
conductance, and lower heart rate than those with closed blinds by 0.1(cid:3)C, 0.12 lS, and 0.98 bpm, respectively. Physiological
responses indicated that participants with a window view were less stressed than those with closed blinds. Short-term working
memory with a window view, compared with closed blinds, improved significantly (by 6%) in the real environment; however, the
increase was not significant in the virtual environment. Short-term working memory was affected by self-reported concentration and
relaxed mood based on visual comfort. Moreover, the physiological responses in the virtual environment were similar to those in the
real environment. This result indicates that a window view improves stressful conditions in both real and virtual environments.

Therefore, the described physiological responses suggested
that participants with closed blinds had more stress than
those with a window view. The PNS in participants with a
window view became more active than in those with closed
blinds; hence, the mean heart rate increased, and RMSSD
and pNN50 decreased. These physiological responses indi-
cate that the window view helps relieve stress. The participants
performed cognitive tests at a lower level of stress because the
physiological responses showed a trend similar to those
observed during environmental exposure (Figures 5 and 6).
Physiological responses of skin temperature, skin conductance,
and HRV were not significantly different between the real and
virtual environments during environmental exposure (Figure 5)
and the cognitive tests (Figure 6).
